title: Content clauses and reported speech
description: Learn how subordinate content clauses are marked, classified, embedded and reported, from that-clauses and whether-clauses to mandative and free indirect speech.
example: She said that the committee would announce its decision after the report had been published.

intro: Start with *She said that the committee would announce its decision*, then drop the *that*: *She said the committee would announce its decision*. The words are almost the same, the meaning is the same, and the grammar has quietly changed shape. In both versions the clause after *said* does the work of a single complement: it names what was said, and it cannot stand on its own.

The clause is not tied to reporting. The same shape appears as the subject of *That they were lying is obvious* and, with a change of host, as the complement of an adjective in *I’m glad that she is right*. What holds these together is not a shared meaning but a shared job: each clause fills a slot that the surrounding construction has opened for it.

This chapter treats the content clause as one construction with several faces: declarative, interrogative and exclamative; subject, object and adjunct; mandative, factive and hypothetical. Once those distinctions are in place, reported speech stops looking like a separate topic. It is what happens when the same clause carries someone else’s words into a new time and a new speaker’s mouth.

blocks.text: Begin with *He knows that she is right*, then try to say *that she is right* on its own. It will not stand: the clause needs a host to lean on. The same dependence shows up when the clause modifies a noun, as in *the report she recommended*, or leans on a connective, as in *Although the paper is poorly written*.

blocks.text: Containment alone tells you nothing. In *Although the paper is poorly written, it contains some good ideas*, the second clause sits inside the sentence but heads the construction. Status is a job, not a location.

Subordinate clauses often advertise themselves. *That* opens a declarative content clause, a missing object opens a relative, and a fronted interrogative phrase with subject-predicator order opens an open interrogative. But the advertisement is optional. *He knows she is right* contains a subordinate clause with the internal shape of a main clause, and only the matrix tells you which is which.

Finite subordinates fall into three classes. Relative clauses carry a gap tied to a nominal, comparatives carry a reduced measure tied to *than* or *as*, and content clauses carry neither special feature. That makes content the default class, the one whose internal grammar most closely resembles a main clause. Non-finite subordinates form a separate system and wait for another chapter.

sections.title: Finite clauses and the content class

blocks.text: *He insists that she be here* looks like a piece of a sentence that has lost its tense. There is no *-s*, no past marker, nothing to agree with *she*. Yet the clause is finite, because the plain form here is the subjunctive, and subjunctives count as primary verb forms. *He thinks that she is here* is finite for the ordinary reason; the two belong to the same class. Non-finite clauses, by contrast, are headed by a gerund-participle, past participle or infinitival plain form, and they lie outside this system.

What separates the three finite subordinate classes is not meaning but what the clause is missing. A relative clause has a gap that takes its interpretation from a nominal. A comparative clause has a reduced measure that takes its interpretation from *than* or *as*. A content clause has neither: it arrives with the full complement structure of a main clause, or with a marker such as *that* or *whether* doing the subordinating.

Content clauses are therefore the ones that look least subordinate. In *I know she is right* nothing inside the clause announces its dependent status; the matrix verb *know* does all the work. Calling the clause subordinate is a statement about its function, not about its shape.

blocks.text: Try to report an order with a content clause and the construction resists. *He said be quiet* does not work as a subordinate construction; an imperative cannot be subordinated that way. Declarative, closed interrogative, open interrogative and exclamative clauses all can. The missing type is a fact about the system, not an accident of vocabulary.

The declarative is the unmarked option, and it comes in two guises: with *that* and without. Closed interrogatives take *whether* or *if*, open interrogatives front a wh-phrase, and exclamatives front *what* or *how*. The clause type is visible in the clause itself, which is why the matrix verb can select for it.

One consequence is easy to miss. Subordinate interrogatives keep subject-predicator order: *I wonder what he does*, never *I wonder what does he do*. A main-clause question inverts; an embedded one does not.

blocks.text: *He knows that you are here* and *He knows you are here* say the same thing. With *that*, the boundary between matrix and subordinate clause is marked; without it, the listener infers it.

Some hosts will not tolerate the marker at all. *If* and *before* take bare declaratives, as in *I’ll do it if you pay me* and *He left before she died*. These are non-expandable. Others are more permissive: *provided* allows both *provided that you pay me* and *provided you pay me*.

Where both forms exist, the choice carries information about register and processing. *That* is likelier in formal prose, after longer or rarer verbs, when the clause is separated from its verb, and when the clause has been moved to the front. Omission is likelier after everyday verbs of thinking and saying, especially in speech.

sections.title: When that must or may be omitted

blocks.text: Move a content clause to the front and the marker stops being optional. *That he really intended to cheat us I still can’t believe* is grammatical; drop *that* and the opening becomes unparseable until the reader reaches *I*. The same demand arises when the clause is an adjunct, and when it follows comparative *than* or *as* and would otherwise be mistaken for a comparative clause.

At the other extreme, *that* can be impossible. *Who does she think is the ringleader?* is fine; *Who does she think that is the ringleader?* is not. The subject of the content clause is a gap, and the fronted *who* must reach it. *That* would sit between the two halves of a single dependency, and the dependency cannot survive the interruption.

Elsewhere the marker comes and goes. Common verbs such as *think*, *say* and *know*, short matrix clauses and casual style all favour omission. Complex vocabulary, distance between verb and clause, and coordination where a second *that* prevents a main-clause reading all favour retention. Nothing in the grammar forces the choice; usage, rhythm and clarity do.

sections.title: Content clauses as subject and extraposed subject

blocks.text: *That they were lying is obvious* is grammatical, and almost nobody says it. English prefers to park a dummy *it* in subject position and send the clause to the end: *It is obvious that they were lying*. The preference grows stronger as the clause gets longer or the predicate gets shorter.
The moved clause is still the subject in meaning. *It* is an empty placeholder, and the clause supplies what the predicate is about.

The same dummy can appear in object position. *They made it clear that the meeting was cancelled* has *it* as object and the clause as an extraposed object; *made* takes *it* as its object, and the clause is related to that object rather than selected directly by the verb.

sections.title: Complements of verbs, nouns, adjectives, and prepositions

blocks.text: *He knows that she is right* is the easy case: a verb taking a clause complement. Change the host and the same clause keeps its shape while its label changes. A noun can take it in *the belief that she is right*, an adjective in *I’m glad that she is right*. A preposition can take an interrogative version, as in *We agreed on whether to go*. The clause does not care; the host decides what the function is.

Not every content clause is selected. *He appealed to us that justice might be done* contains a clause expressing a desired outcome, and here *that* is obligatory. The *so ... that* construction is a different special case: *It was so cold that the lake froze* pairs a degree expression with a clause stating its consequence.

“Object clause” survives in older descriptions, but it fits only a minority of the examples. A content clause can be subject, complement of a noun, adjective or preposition, extraposed, or an adjunct. The function has to be read off the matrix construction; the label cannot be carried over from Latin grammar and applied wholesale.

blocks.text: *He asked whether she was ill* and *He asked if she was ill* are both closed interrogative content clauses. The difference is the marker, not the clause type. Open interrogatives work differently: they front a wh-phrase and leave the rest of the clause in declarative order.

*Whether* and *if* overlap, but only one of them travels well. *Whether* survives after a preposition (*We discussed whether to go*), in subject position (*Whether he comes is uncertain*), and in exhaustive conditionals (*whether you like it or not*). *If* is barred from those positions in Standard English. The restriction is grammatical, not a matter of tone.

Beyond complements, interrogative clauses appear as supplements, as complements of adjectives such as *uncertain*, and in infinitival form after verbs like *know* and *decide* (*I don’t know what to do*). They also occur ungoverned, as in *Whether you like it or not, we’re going*, where the clause quantifies over alternatives and the matrix holds whichever one obtains. Dubitatives such as *I doubt whether he will come* put the same clause to work expressing doubt.

blocks.text: The same interrogative clause can point in two directions. *I asked whether she was coming* leaves the issue open; *I know whether she is coming* closes it, naming an answer the speaker already has. Verbs of asking and wondering tend one way, verbs of knowing the other.

Doubt has its own construction. *I doubt whether he will come* and *It’s doubtful whether they can finish* present the embedded question as unresolved, and the doubt attaches to the clause rather than to a negative answer. Infinitival interrogatives are common after *know*, *decide*, *wonder* and *ask*, as in *She asked how to apply*.

*Whether you like it or not, we’re going* has no governing predicate at all. The clause is an adjunct, and it quantifies over two alternatives: the matrix clause is presented as holding under either. This is a conditional use of an interrogative clause, not a complement, and it is why the construction can stand at the front of the sentence with nothing to license it.

blocks.text: *You know what a liar he is* contains a *what*, but nothing is being asked. The clause reports an exclamation, and the matrix verb *know* presents it as something the addressee already appreciates. Verbs of realizing, remembering and reporting license the same pattern, and the clause stays close to an open interrogative in form while differing from it in meaning and distribution.

Inside the clause the exclamative phrase moves to the front. In *You know what a liar he is*, *what a liar* occupies the prenuclear position and *he is* follows as the nucleus. The clause is subordinate, but its exclamative type is intact.

Exclamative content clauses tend to appear after factive or semi-factive predicates. *I know how difficult it was* presupposes that it was difficult; *I wonder how difficult it was* does not. The predicate decides whether the exclamation is offered as shared knowledge or left as an open question.

blocks.text: Mandative constructions take a requirement and put it in a clause. *It is important that she be told* uses the subjunctive; *It is important that she should be told* uses *should*; *It is important that she is told* uses the indicative. Verbs such as *insist*, *demand* and *recommend* behave the same way, and the choice among the three forms is partly regional and partly stylistic.

The subjunctive is easy to misclassify because the verb looks bare. *She be told* has no agreement and no tense ending, but the clause is finite: the plain form is the subjunctive marker, and subjunctive clauses belong with finite clauses, not with infinitivals. The absence of inflection is the signal, not the absence of finiteness.

Tense can also be used for distance rather than time. *I wish she were here* puts *were* in a clause about the present, and *If he knew, he would tell us* uses a past form to mark a hypothesis. Present tense can point to the future in a content clause, as in *I hope she arrives tomorrow*. Factivity is a separate dimension: *I know that she left* presupposes that she left, while *I believe that she left* leaves the question open.

blocks.text: *She said that the committee would announce its decision* reports words without reproducing them. There is a reporting verb, a content clause, and a set of adjustments: the tense, the pronouns, and the time and place words all shift to fit the reporter’s position. Nothing is quoted.

Backshift is the most conspicuous adjustment. *She said she was tired* uses a past tense even if the tiredness was present when she spoke; the past marks the report’s perspective, not necessarily past time. Deixis shifts with it: *now* becomes *then*, *today* becomes *that day*, *here* becomes *there*, and *I* becomes *she*.
Backshift is not a mechanical rule. *She said she is tired* is fine when the state still holds; the choice depends on how the speaker frames the report.

check.prompt: What is backshift in indirect reported speech?

options.text: The use of a past tense to mark anteriority relative to the report.
options.feedback: It is a perspective shift, not a simple change of event time.
Quotation marks are characteristic of direct report.
That is optional in many reports but not the definition of backshift.

blocks.text: *She said, ‘I am tired.’* keeps the original words and the original deictic centre. *I* still means the person who spoke, *now* still means the time of speaking, and *here* still means the place. Quotation marks are the visible sign of that retention, but the pronouns and adverbs are what do the work.

Free indirect speech drops the reporting clause and lets the character’s perspective leak into third-person past narration. *She was tired. Tomorrow she would leave.* The pronouns and tense are the narrator’s; the evaluation and the deictic orientation are the character’s. The effect is a voice that belongs to neither fully.

Free direct speech keeps more of the original wording, often without quotation marks. The boundary between it and free indirect style is a matter of degree, and the choice controls how close the reader stands to the character.

blocks.text: By now the content clause should look less like a single construction than like a family. Its members can be declarative, interrogative or exclamative, but never imperative; they can be marked by *that*, *whether*, *if*, a fronted phrase, or nothing at all; and they can serve as subject, complement, adjunct or supplement.

*That* is required when the clause is subject, preposed or an adjunct, impossible when a subject gap is linked to a fronted phrase, and optional elsewhere. Interrogatives divide into question-oriented, answer-oriented and dubitative uses; exclamatives follow factive or semi-factive predicates.

Mood and factivity decide how the content is presented. Mandatives choose among subjunctive, *should* and indicative; modal preterite and irrealis mark distance; factive predicates presuppose their complements. Reported speech then adds a further layer, since indirect report shifts deixis and tense, direct report preserves them, and free indirect style holds both in suspension.

blocks.title: A content-clause checklist
blocks.text: Identify the clause boundaries and its function in the matrix. Decide whether it is declarative, interrogative or exclamative. Check whether that is present, optional or excluded. Then examine mood, factivity and the deictic shifts of reported speech.

check.prompt: Which statement correctly describes content clauses?

options.text: They are the default finite subordinate class and can be declarative, interrogative or exclamative.
options.feedback: Imperative content clauses do not occur.

options.text: They are always introduced by that.
options.feedback: Bare declaratives and whether/if clauses are also content clauses.

options.text: They can only function as objects.
options.feedback: They can be subjects, complements, adjuncts and supplements.

worked: Take *She said that the committee would announce its decision after the report had been published*. The matrix clause is *She said that ...*; its complement is the declarative content clause *that the committee would announce its decision after the report had been published*. The clause is expanded with that and functions as the object of said.

Inside the content clause, the past-tense *would* is a future-in-the-past form, and *had been published* is a past perfect locating the publication before the announcement. The report is indirect: the original speaker’s words are not quoted, and the deictic centre has shifted to the narrator’s past perspective.
application: Find the subordinate clause and identify its function in the matrix. Then classify its type: declarative, closed interrogative, open interrogative or exclamative. Check whether it is finite or non-finite and whether it is marked by that, whether, if or a fronted phrase.

Next, examine the marker. Is that obligatory, optional or excluded? Does the clause function as subject, extraposed subject, complement of a verb, noun, adjective or preposition, or adjunct? The position and the governing item determine the possibilities.

Finally, interpret mood and report. Is the clause mandative, modal, factive or hypothetical? If it reports speech, identify the deictic shifts and whether the report is direct, indirect or free indirect. The same content can be presented from different perspectives.
reveal: In *She said that the committee would announce its decision after the report had been published*, the content clause is declarative and functions as the object of said. It is expanded with that. Would is a future-in-the-past modal, and had been published is a past perfect marking anteriority to the announcement.
recap: Content clauses are the default finite subordinate class. They carry declarative, interrogative or exclamative type and function as subjects, complements, adjuncts or supplements. That is obligatory in some positions, excluded in others, and optional in the default case.

Interrogative content clauses use whether or if and occur in question-oriented, answer-oriented and dubitative constructions. Exclamative content clauses use what or how. Mood, factivity and reported speech shape how the content is interpreted and attributed.

self_check.question: What are the three classes of finite subordinate clause?

self_check.question: When is that obligatory in a content clause?

self_check.question: When must that be omitted?
self_check.answer: When the subject of the content clause is realised by a gap in an unbounded dependency construction.

self_check.question: What is the difference between whether and if in content clauses?
self_check.answer: Both can introduce closed interrogative content clauses, but whether occurs after prepositions and as subject, where if is excluded.

self_check.question: What is backshift in reported speech?
self_check.answer: The use of a past tense to mark anteriority relative to the reporting time, often with shifts in pronouns and time or place expressions.
